title: What an IP Risk Score Really Means
author: IP Ready
excerpt: Every scan ends with a number from 0 to 100. Here is what feeds it, how to read each band, and why it moves.
body:
Every IP Ready scan ends the same way: a number between 0 and 100. It is tempting to treat that number as a verdict, but a risk score is closer to a diagnosis — a structured estimate built from public signals, each of which you can inspect and most of which you can change. This guide walks through what actually feeds the score, how to read each band, and why the same address can score differently next week.

Where the Number Comes From

A risk score is a weighted read of several independent signal groups:

  • Reputation and blacklists — whether the address appears on DNS blocklists or has a recent abuse history reported by the community.
  • Network type — whether the IP is registered to a home ISP, a mobile carrier, or a commercial datacenter. Platforms weight this heavily because it correlates with who controls the connection.
  • Location consistency — whether the registered geography, timezone, and routing of the address agree with each other.
  • Hosting signals — whether the ASN belongs to a cloud or hosting provider rather than a consumer ISP.

No single signal decides the score. A datacenter IP with a clean reputation scores better than a residential IP with an abuse record — but all else equal, the residential address starts from a better position.

How to Read Each Band

BandWhat it meansWhat to do
0–29 · Low riskSignals are clean and consistent with a normal user connection.Keep the current setup; re-scan when you switch networks.
30–59 · Medium riskSome signals conflict — often network type or a stale blacklist entry.Read the flagged signals in the report and address them one at a time.
60–100 · High riskMultiple signal groups disagree or carry negative history.Expect friction on strict platforms; replace the exit IP or its type.

Why the Score Moves

Reputation databases update continuously. Blacklist entries expire and get re-added, VPN endpoints churn, carriers renumber their pools, and hosting providers hand ranges to new tenants. That is why two scans of the same address a week apart can disagree — and why re-scanning after switching networks, VPN locations, or devices is not paranoia but hygiene.

A risk score is where the conversation starts, not where it ends. Run a scan, read the signals behind the number, and treat each one as a lever you can actually pull.
